newsitem.title: ITALY: Food summit, dominated by Zaire, awaits Castro.
newsitem.headline: Food summit, dominated by Zaire, awaits Castro.

text.p: Cuba's Fidel Castro will take centre stage on Friday at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit dominated so far by the tragedy in Zaire -- if he shows up.

An official order of speakers named the world's longest-serving communist leader among 37 heads of state or government scheduled to address the summit at the Rome headquarters of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation.
Castro could also use his visit for an historic audience with Pope John Paul and diplomatic sources said he would meet Italian leaders as well.

Cuba, traditionally secretive about the movements of its leader, has not confirmed Castro will attend. The 70-year-old veteran revolutionary had still not arrived in the Italian capital by early Friday morning, airport officials said.

Despite his absence so far from the summit, Castro was given a prominent role as one of six vice-chairmen of the five-day meeting when it got under way on Wednesday with a pledge to work to halve global hunger in 20 years.
The summit offers Castro, listed to speak at around 1300 GMT, a golden opportunity to blast a 34-year-old U.S. trade embargo and the recent Helms-Burton law designed to squeeze him out of power.
The U.N. General Assembly voted on Tuesday by its biggest majority in five years to lift the ban. Cuba hailed it as a victory for its revolution and proof of Washington's isolation.
At the summit on Thursday, Libyan Agriculture Minister Ali Ben Romdhan attacked the use of sanctions. A further blast was expected from Iraqi Vice-President Taha Mohieddin Ma'rouf.
President Omar Hassan Al-Bashir of Sudan, another country under U.N. sanctions, was also due to speak on Friday.

A document entitled "Food for All" released by the Cuban delegation on Thursday painted the Caribbean island as a socialist success story despite the U.S. embargo, falling exports and an inability to feed its 11 million people.

The document said the Helms-Burton law, giving Cuban-Americans the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the Cuban government from exiles after the 1959 revolution, had worsened the blockade.
The summit has been dominated so far by African efforts to send an international force into eastern Zaire to help over a million starving Rwandan and Burundian refugees.

"The fate of one million human beings is being played out amid the total indifference of the international community and the governments of the places these people are from," said Zaire's Deputy Prime Minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda.
He said on Thursday that all aid should be sent to Rwanda and Burundi to encourage refugees to go back there.

The situation was sure to be discussed further on Friday, with Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi and Burundi's Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira among a score of African leaders scheduled to address delegates.

Castro is expected to spend the weekend in Rome, diplomatic sources said. The main debate has been on whether he might meet the Pope, 76, who crusaded against communism in his native Poland and in the Soviet bloc.

The Vatican has made clear it is waiting for Cuba to request an audience, which religious sources said appeared most likely to take place on Saturday because of the Pope's other engagements. It said it had still not received any request.
A meeting between the two men would cement improving relations between Cuba and the Roman Catholic Church and could pave the way for the "Pilgrim Pope" to visit Cuba next year.
